nameStory: The Atlantic Macoma gets its name from its distribution along the Atlantic coast, while 'Macoma' comes from a Native American word meaning 'clam.' The genus name has been used since the 1800s when scientists first began systematically cataloging these small but important shellfish.
description: The Atlantic Macoma is a small, thin-shelled clam that lives buried in muddy and sandy bottoms of estuaries and shallow coastal waters. Its oval shell typically measures 1-2 inches long and has a distinctive chalky white to pale pink color. Unlike the thick, heavy shells of quahogs or steamers, the Macoma's shell feels delicate and lightweight in your hand. This little bivalve is an important food source for shorebirds and bottom-feeding fish.

idTips.label: Thin, fragile shell
idTips.description: The shell feels remarkably thin and lightweight compared to other clams, almost papery, and can break easily when handled

idTips.label: Oval shape with pointed end
idTips.description: Shell is distinctly oval rather than round, with one end more pointed than the other, creating an elongated teardrop profile

idTips.label: Chalky white to pink color
idTips.description: Fresh shells have a matte, chalky texture that's white to pale pink, without the glossy shine of many other clams

idTips.label: Fine growth rings
idTips.description: Delicate concentric rings circle the shell from the hinge, feeling slightly raised under your fingertip like tiny ridges

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Typically fits comfortably in your palm at 1-2 inches long, much smaller than most edible clams

habitat: Look for Atlantic Macomas in muddy or sandy bottoms of salt marshes, estuaries, and protected shallow bays throughout New England's coast. They prefer areas where fresh and salt water mix, often in the same spots where you'd find fiddler crabs and ribbed mussels. Live specimens burrow 2-4 inches deep in the sediment, but their shells commonly wash up on mudflats and beaches after storms.

seasonality.spring: Empty shells become more visible on mudflats as winter storms subside and ice melts. This is when you're most likely to find fresh, intact specimens washed up after spring tides.
seasonality.summer: Peak time for finding shells on beaches and mudflats during low tides. Live clams are actively feeding just below the surface in warm, nutrient-rich waters.
seasonality.fall: Shell collection remains good through autumn storms. Look for concentrations of shells in wrack lines where waves have deposited them.
seasonality.winter: Fewer shells visible due to ice cover in northern areas, but southern New England beaches may still yield specimens after winter storms.

funFact: Atlantic Macomas are incredible water filters - a single clam can process over 5 gallons of water per day, helping to keep coastal waters clean by removing tiny particles and algae from the water column.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other small tellins, but the Atlantic Macoma's distinctively thin, almost translucent shell and oval shape with pointed end sets it apart. Remember: if it feels heavy for its size, it's probably not a Macoma - these shells are surprisingly lightweight.
contextualKnowledge: While called 'Atlantic' Macoma, this species actually occurs on both coasts - Pacific populations were once considered the same species. The scientific name 'petalum' means 'petal-like,' referring to the shell's delicate, thin appearance that resembles a flower petal.
compareHints: Since Atlantic Macoma is the only Macoma species commonly found in New England, compare it with other small tellins in the family. Unlike the more circular tellins, Atlantic Macoma has a distinctly elongated oval shape. Its shell is also thinner and more fragile than most related species, and lacks the bright colors sometimes seen in other tellin clams.
